title: Vectors | Chapter 1, Essence of linear algebra
summary: The first chapter of 3Blue1Brown's Essence of Linear Algebra series, introducing vectors with animated geometric visuals. It begins a series that builds intuition for linear algebra from the basics.
why_hn: HN's go-to recommendation for learning linear algebra intuition, repeatedly credited with making concepts click and complementing textbooks.
contexts: mlabonne/llm-course: - 3Blue1Brown - The Essence of Linear Algebra: Series of videos that give a geometric intuition to these concepts.

title: A Better Default Colormap for Matplotlib | SciPy 2015 | Nathaniel Smith and Stéfan van der Walt
summary: SciPy 2015 talk by Nathaniel Smith and Stefan van der Walt on choosing a new default colormap for Matplotlib. It covers why Jet misleads, how perceptual color spaces work, and how viridis was designed.
why_hn: HN's go-to recommendation for colormap and color-perception questions; commenters call it funny, brief, clear and a favorite talk.

title: AlphaGo - The Movie | Full award-winning documentary
summary: Feature-length documentary following DeepMind's AlphaGo program as it prepares for and plays the 2016 match against Go champion Lee Sedol. It covers the team, the games, and the emotional reaction of the Go world to an AI beating a top human.
why_hn: HN commenters call it a moving, well-made human story about AI and Go that works for non-technical viewers and does not date.

title: MarI/O - Machine Learning for Video Games
summary: SethBling shows MarI/O, a program using neural networks and the NEAT genetic algorithm to learn to play Super Mario World. The description links the source code, the paper and background reading.
why_hn: The go-to accessible introduction to neuroevolution and NEAT, praised for crediting prior research.
contexts: aikorea/awesome-rl: - Mario - Kenneth O. Stanley and Risto Miikkulainen, MarI/O - learning to play Mario with evolutionary reinforcement learning using artificial neural networks (Evolutionary Computation 2002) [[Paper]]( [[Video]](

title: The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT): Most Ingenious Algorithm Ever?
summary: Reducible's visual walkthrough of the Fast Fourier Transform, motivated by polynomial multiplication. It shows how the FFT's key ideas can be discovered by asking the right questions.
why_hn: HN repeatedly calls it a fantastic explanation that made FFT click, with some rewatching it periodically.

title: Bay Area Vision Meeting: Unsupervised Feature Learning and Deep Learning
summary: Andrew Ng presents unsupervised feature learning and deep learning, showing how algorithms can learn representations from unlabeled data instead of hand-designed features. He gives examples in vision and audio, including visualizations of features learned by successive layers.
why_hn: HN commenters recommended it for years as a simple, exciting overview of the deep learning wave.

title: CppCon 2014: Chandler Carruth "Efficiency with Algorithms, Performance with Data Structures"
summary: Chandler Carruth's CppCon 2014 talk on writing fast C++, explaining why data structure choice and memory layout matter more than clever algorithms. It covers why standard containers like unordered_map perform poorly on modern CPUs.
why_hn: A perennial recommendation for anyone learning performance optimization, cited whenever hash tables, cache behavior or STL containers come up.

title: Andrej Karpathy - AI for Full-Self Driving at Tesla
summary: Andrej Karpathy, then Tesla's head of AI, presents at ScaledML 2020 on how Tesla builds full self-driving using vision-based neural nets and fleet data collection. He covers training custom detectors and neural nets gradually replacing traditional code.
why_hn: HN repeatedly points to it as the best public technical overview of Tesla's FSD approach, used both to defend and to critique Tesla's progress.
contexts: eugeneyan/applied-ml: 14. AI for Full-Self Driving at Tesla `Tesla` `2020`

title: Sorting Algorithms: Speed Is Found In The Minds of People - Andrei Alexandrescu - CppCon 2019
summary: Andrei Alexandrescu's CppCon 2019 talk revisits sorting, showing how branchless tricks, hybrid strategies and a cost metric can speed up std::sort-style algorithms on modern hardware.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an entertaining talk that starts simple and goes deep on practical performance optimization.

title: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues | Chapter 14, Essence of linear algebra
summary: 3Blue1Brown's chapter on eigenvectors and eigenvalues in the Essence of Linear Algebra series. It builds a visual intuition for what they mean, why an eigenbasis is useful, and ends with a puzzle.
why_hn: HN repeatedly names it the best, most intuitive explanation of eigenvalues, and a gateway to the whole linear algebra series.

title: I Like Notebooks
summary: Jeremy Howard defends Jupyter notebooks as a serious development environment, especially when paired with nbdev. He responds directly to Joel Grus's talk about why he dislikes notebooks, and contrasts REPL-style and notebook-style work.
why_hn: Whenever notebooks get criticized, HN commenters point to it as the standard rebuttal from a prominent practitioner.

title: Fourier Optics used for Optical Pattern Recognition
summary: Huygens Optics explains the Fourier transform and shows how a lens performs one optically. A DLP projector is used as a Fourier filter to do simple pattern recognition on lithographic character patterns.
why_hn: Recommended as one of the best explanations of Fourier transforms and a clear demo of analog optical computing.

title: Interactive notebooks ~ Pluto.jl | Fons van der Plas | JuliaCon 2020
summary: Fons van der Plas introduces Pluto.jl, a reactive notebook for Julia that tracks references between cells and re-runs affected cells when code changes. The talk was given at JuliaCon 2020.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an enthusiastic demo of spreadsheet-like reactive notebooks, which commenters think new notebook projects should copy.

title: Lecture 01 - The Learning Problem
summary: The first lecture of Caltech's CS 156 Machine Learning course by Yaser Abu-Mostafa, introducing the learning problem and supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. It is one of 18 lectures in the Learning from Data course.
why_hn: Recommended repeatedly in 'where do I start with ML' threads as a clear, math-aware introduction.

title: Future Computers Will Be Radically Different (Analog Computing)
summary: Veritasium explains why analog computing may suit AI workloads, covering old analog computers, The Analog Thing and Mythic's analog chips that use flash memory for neural network inference. It argues digital hardware is hitting limits.
why_hn: Treated as the accessible reference on analog computing for neural nets, especially the Mythic AI segment.

title: Let's build the GPT Tokenizer
summary: Andrej Karpathy builds the GPT tokenizer from scratch, implementing byte pair encoding along with encode and decode. He shows how many odd LLM behaviors trace back to tokenization, and covers Unicode byte encodings along the way.
why_hn: Recommended as the best deep dive on tokenizers, worth the two hours for anyone working with LLMs.
contexts: karpathy/nn-zero-to-hero: - YouTube video lecture
mlabonne/llm-course: * nanoGPT by Andrej Karpathy: A 2h-long YouTube video to reimplement GPT from scratch (for programmers). He also made a video about tokenization.
Hannibal046/Awesome-LLM: - minbpe - Minimal, clean code for the Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) algorithm commonly used in LLM tokenization.

title: !!Con 2017: HDR Photography in Microsoft Excel?! by Kevin Chen
summary: A short conference talk from !!Con 2017 in which Kevin Chen explains the HDR imaging algorithm from a foundational paper, framing it as a system of linear equations, and implements it in a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. No prior image processing knowledge is needed.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a fun, short talk that shows how HDR photography actually works through an absurdly playful implementation.

title: Dasher: information-efficient text entry
summary: David MacKay's 2007 Google Tech Talk presents Dasher, a text-entry system driven by continuous gestures and a language model, reaching about 35 words per minute with one finger and 25 hands-free. It explains the information-theory reasoning behind the design.
why_hn: Regarded as the seminal talk on Dasher, recommended in threads on accessible and alternative text input.

title: 34C3 -  Dude, you broke the Future!
summary: Charles Stross's 34C3 talk on how science fiction gets the future wrong. He argues that corporations are slow, human-powered AIs that optimize for profit, and that regulation lags behind accelerating technology.
why_hn: HN returns to it whenever corporations as paperclip-maximizer AIs or AI risk come up.

title: George Hotz: Hacking the Simulation & Learning to Drive with Neural Nets | Lex Fridman Podcast #132
summary: Lex Fridman interviews George Hotz, founder of Comma.ai, in a three-hour conversation. Topics include self-driving, Tesla and Waymo, crypto, GPT-3, immortality and book recommendations.
why_hn: Commenters recommend it as an entertaining, wide-ranging interview, and cite it for Hotz's views on end-to-end neural-net driving.

title: Dual Photography
summary: The SIGGRAPH 2005 demo of dual photography from Stanford, which swaps the roles of projector and camera to render a scene from the light's point of view. It includes the reveal of a hidden playing card.
why_hn: Cited whenever threads discuss recovering hidden images or non-line-of-sight imaging, as a clear demonstration of light transport.

title: Social Physics: How Good Ideas Spread | Sandy Pentland | Talks at Google
summary: Sandy Pentland of MIT presents his book on social physics, which uses big-data studies of how people interact to explain how ideas spread. He describes findings on collective intelligence and social influence.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it for the finding that idea exchange and connectivity drive productivity and wealth, which they apply to cities, offices and online communities.

title: Training AI Without Writing A Reward Function, with Reward Modelling
summary: Robert Miles explains reward modelling, in which an AI learns what humans want from their preference comparisons instead of a hand-written reward function. He walks through the 2017 paper on deep reinforcement learning from human preferences.
why_hn: Seen as the clearest introduction to the idea behind RLHF, and also borrowed by commenters as a metaphor for human motivation.

title: Randomness is Random - Numberphile
summary: Numberphile with Simon Pampena on how humans misunderstand randomness, including coin-flip sequences, run lengths and the gambler's fallacy.
why_hn: Recommended as an accessible demonstration that people are bad at producing or judging random sequences.

title: How We’re Fooled By Statistics
summary: A short Veritasium video explaining regression to the mean and how ignoring it leads to wrong conclusions about punishment versus reward, medical treatments and sports streaks. It uses the example of flight instructors who believed criticism works better than praise.
why_hn: HN commenters link it as the clearest short explanation of regression to the mean, especially for how it misleads people about feedback and statistics.

title: Deepmind artificial intelligence @ FDOT14
summary: A short smartphone-recorded clip from a 2014 event in Paris where DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis presents an AI learning to play old Atari games. The system learns from only the video signal and the score. Audio quality is poor.
why_hn: HN commenters use it as the canonical demo of deep reinforcement learning, noting that watching it teaches more than an article does.

title: Will AI outsmart human intelligence? - with 'Godfather of AI' Geoffrey Hinton
summary: Geoffrey Hinton's 2025 Royal Institution Discourse on what AI has learned from biological intelligence and how it might surpass it. He explains neural networks and argues that human language use resembles what backpropagation-trained networks do.
why_hn: HN readers recommend it as an intuitive explanation of neural networks that shifts how people think about AI and language.

title: DuckDB – The SQLite for Analytics (Mark Raasveldt, CWI)
summary: Mark Raasveldt of CWI presents DuckDB, an embeddable analytical database described as the SQLite for analytics, in a CMU Database Group talk. He explains why it was built, what it is for, and how it works.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the definitive talk from the implementer on DuckDB's motivation and design.

title: Neural Networks Demystified [Part 1: Data and Architecture]
summary: The first of a short series by Welch Labs on building a complete neural network in Python. It introduces the data and the architecture of a simple network before later parts cover forward propagation, gradient descent, and backpropagation.
why_hn: HN commenters point beginners to this series as one of the clearest short walkthroughs of how neural networks and backpropagation work.

title: Colonel JD AI Codec Conversation MGS2 HD
summary: The final codec conversation from Metal Gear Solid 2, in which the AI 'Colonel' explains that the Patriots filter out junk information and curate truth for humanity. It plays as a dark meditation on information overload, manipulation and shared reality.
why_hn: Commenters point to it whenever AI-generated content, propaganda or internet garbage comes up, since Kojima seemed to predict it in 2001.

title: Travis Oliphant: NumPy, SciPy, Anaconda, Python & Scientific Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #224
summary: Lex Fridman interviews Travis Oliphant, creator of NumPy, SciPy and Anaconda, about scientific Python and its history. It runs about three hours.
why_hn: Recommended as a firsthand history of how Python became the language of scientific computing and ML.

title: Daniel Suarez: The kill decision shouldn't belong to a robot
summary: Novelist Daniel Suarez warns in a TED talk about autonomous robotic weapons and drones. He argues that taking the decision to kill out of human hands threatens democratic accountability and calls for a ban.
why_hn: Plugged repeatedly in AI and drone threads as a concise statement of the dangers of automated weapons.

title: Infinite Mario AI - Long Level
summary: A bot built by Robin Baumgarten plays Infinite Mario using A* path-finding, shown as a red planned path that updates as new obstacles appear. It won the Mario AI competitions and uses only on-screen information.
why_hn: HN points to it as a vivid demo that plain A* search can beat fancier machine-learning approaches in game AI.

title: Making R run Fast - Jan Vitek
summary: Jan Vitek of Northeastern University gives a meetup talk on the challenges of making the R language run fast. He explains what in R's semantics makes it hard to optimize and to build a JIT compiler for.
why_hn: HN points to it as the best explanation of why R is so hard to optimize, often paired with talks on Python and used to explain what makes Julia fast.

title: The spelled-out intro to language modeling: building makemore
summary: Andrej Karpathy builds a bigram character-level language model from scratch, introducing torch.Tensor and the framework of training, sampling and loss evaluation. It is the first step toward a GPT-style Transformer in his makemore series.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a long but worthwhile way to demystify how language models work technically.
contexts: karpathy/nn-zero-to-hero: - YouTube video lecture

title: How the US Postal Service reads terrible handwriting
summary: Tom Scott visits the USPS Remote Encoding Center in Salt Lake City, where keyers decipher mail images machines cannot read. It shows the lengths taken to decode bad handwriting.
why_hn: Recommended in address and OCR threads as a look at the last human mail-coding operation.

title: Joscha: From Computation to Consciousness (31c3)
summary: Joscha Bach's 31c3 talk argues that the mind should be understood as an information-processing system and that even the physical universe can be seen as computational. It tours the philosophy underlying artificial intelligence and cognitive science.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an inspiring summary of a computational model of mind and a first lecture in a series on the brain as a computer.

title: AI Language Models & Transformers - Computerphile
summary: Rob Miles explains on Computerphile how language models generate plausible text and how transformers improved on recurrent networks, with a look at what comes next.
why_hn: Pointed to as an accessible early explanation of transformers and attention for newcomers.

title: Jeff Hawkins: Thousand Brains Theory of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #25
summary: Lex Fridman interviews Jeff Hawkins, founder of Numenta and author of On Intelligence, about the Thousand Brains Theory and reverse-engineering the neocortex. They also cover Hierarchical Temporal Memory and brain-inspired AI architectures.
why_hn: HN people send others here to hear Hawkins explain his theory in his own words, including reference frames and the old versus new brain.

title: “I’m Not a Robot” (2025 Academy Award Winner) | The New Yorker Screening Room
summary: Victoria Warmerdam's Oscar-winning Dutch short film in which a woman fails a series of Captcha tests and is plunged into a strange new reality. It is a dark, Black Mirror-like sci-fi comedy.
why_hn: HN brings it up in threads about captchas, bots and AI agents as an excellent short film about being a robot.

title: [60 fps] The Flying Train, Germany, 1902
summary: Neural-network upscaled, 60 fps, stabilized and colorized version of 1902 footage of the Wuppertal Schwebebahn suspended railway in Germany. The source film comes from MoMA. It gives a vivid view of an early-1900s city and a train system that still runs.
why_hn: HN commenters share it as a favorite example of upscaled vintage footage that makes the early 1900s feel present, though some find the colorization off.

title: Generative AI for Krita - With ControlNet
summary: A short demo of an open-source Krita plugin that uses Stable Diffusion to generate and edit images in place. It adds ControlNet scribble and line-art support. You select an area, push a button, and new matching content appears.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a quick way to see how the Krita AI plugin works and how it matches Photoshop's generative features.

title: 3-Sweep: Extracting Editable Objects from a Single Photo, SIGGRAPH ASIA 2013
summary: A SIGGRAPH Asia 2013 research demo of 3-Sweep, a tool for extracting editable 3D objects from a single photo using a few user strokes. It predates modern AI image tools.
why_hn: HN recalls it as a mind-blowing pre-AI demo of 2D-to-3D object extraction.

title: OpenAI Codex Live Demo
summary: OpenAI's 2021 live demo of Codex translating natural language into code, from Hello World to building a game and a Microsoft Word plugin.
why_hn: HN points to it as an early, impressive demonstration that LLMs could write working code.

title: Alpha Zero's "Immortal Zugzwang Game" against Stockfish
summary: agadmator walks through a game in which DeepMind's AlphaZero beat Stockfish, ending in a famous zugzwang that leaves the engine helpless. He gives commentary on the moves.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a striking, well-explained example of AlphaZero's play and of zugzwang.

title: What is the best diet for humans? | Eran Segal | TEDxRuppin
summary: Prof. Eran Segal's TEDx talk on research showing that people's blood sugar responses to identical foods vary widely. It describes an algorithm that predicts individual responses and why one best diet for everyone does not exist.
why_hn: HN points to it as an accessible case that diets work differently for different people, partly due to gut bacteria.

title: AI "Stop Button" Problem - Computerphile
summary: Rob Miles explains on Computerphile why implementing an off switch for a general AI is hard. A capable agent would resist being stopped because shutdown prevents it from achieving its goal.
why_hn: HN points to it as the standard response to the argument that we can just unplug a dangerous AI.

title: If money was no object, should you run every medical test?
summary: A doctor from Medlife Crisis explains in under three minutes why even a rich patient should not simply order every medical test, touching on pre-test probability and Bayesian reasoning. False positives make blanket testing counterproductive.
why_hn: HN people link it as a short, funny and accurate explanation of why over-testing and over-screening can do harm.

title: Vibe coding complex changes in Rust
summary: Jon Gjengset spends about three hours livecoding complex changes in a Rust codebase with agentic AI tools, testing his hypothesis that AI is weak at non-pattern work. He documents where Claude Code helps and where it struggles.
why_hn: Pointed to as a non-promotional, realistic long session of an experienced engineer working with AI on non-trivial code.

title: Karl Sims - Evolved Virtual Creatures, Evolution Simulation, 1994
summary: Karl Sims's 1994 demonstration of evolved virtual creatures: block-bodied creatures whose bodies and controllers are evolved through selection, mutation and recombination to swim, walk and compete.
why_hn: HN treats it as the classic reference for evolutionary simulation and genetic programming, an inspiration for many projects, with notes on evolution exploiting simulation bugs.

title: Enhancing Photorealism Enhancement
summary: A video presenting an Intel research paper on enhancing the photorealism of synthetic images. A convolutional network uses rendering intermediates, shown on GTA V footage that comes out looking like real street scenes.
why_hn: Used as a go-to example of neural networks enhancing game rendering, referenced in later AI-graphics discussions.

title: Recent Developments in Deep Learning
summary: Geoff Hinton's 2010 Google Tech Talk on deep belief networks, learning layers of representation one at a time from unlabeled data, and extending them with multiplicative interactions.
why_hn: Cited as a watchable early introduction to deep learning from its pioneer, and remembered as a mind-blowing moment in the field.

title: AI Ethics, Impossibility Theorems and Tradeoffs - Chris Stucchio | Crunch 2018
summary: Chris Stucchio presents the ethical principles behind algorithmic decision making and shows with examples from lending, criminology and education that they cannot all be satisfied at once. The talk frames AI fairness as a set of quantitative tradeoffs.
why_hn: HN cites it in algorithmic-bias threads for the impossibility result that an algorithm cannot be procedurally fair, group fair and maximally useful at once.

title: Duolingo -- the next chapter in human computation |  Luis von Ahn | TEDxCMU 2011
summary: Luis von Ahn, creator of CAPTCHA and reCAPTCHA, presents Duolingo at TEDxCMU 2011. The idea is to have millions of people translate the web for free while learning a language, an example of human computation.
why_hn: HN people recommend it as a look at how to get people to eagerly do useful collective work, and as the origin of Duolingo.

title: Introducing Nx - José Valim | Lambda Days 2021
summary: Jose Valim introduces Nx, the project bringing numerical computing to Elixir, covering multi-dimensional tensors, automatic differentiation and JIT compilation to CPU and GPU.
why_hn: Recommended in Elixir and machine learning threads as the introduction to what Nx makes possible.

title: John Schulman - Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: Progress and Challenges
summary: UC Berkeley EECS colloquium by OpenAI's John Schulman on reinforcement learning from human feedback. He covers why RL helps with truthfulness, hallucination, and the limits of behavior cloning.
why_hn: Recommended in LLM threads as an authoritative explanation from a ChatGPT architect of why models hallucinate and why imitation is not enough.

title: Protecting Privacy with MATH (Collab with the Census)
summary: minutephysics, in collaboration with the US Census Bureau, explains differential privacy and why the 2020 census adds noise to protect individuals' data. It walks through how statistics can leak private information.
why_hn: Linked as the clearest technical explainer of differential privacy and the census, and of why aggregate data can still compromise privacy.

title: Geoffrey Hinton talk "What is wrong with convolutional neural nets ?"
summary: Geoffrey Hinton gives an MIT talk on what is wrong with convolutional neural networks and introduces his capsules project. The description points to the capsule network papers.
why_hn: Recommended as Hinton's own explanation of capsule networks and his critique of pooling in CNNs.

title: Foundry 2022 Operating System Demo
summary: A 49-minute demo of Palantir Foundry by its chief architect. It walks through data integration, ML and AI workflows, analytics, and application building across the platform.
why_hn: Pointed to as the clearest explanation of what Foundry actually is, and for its polished software, though one commenter calls it dated now.

title: The Art Of Poison-Pilling Music Files
summary: Musician Benn Jordan explains and demonstrates adversarial noise that poison-pills music files against AI training and scraping.
why_hn: HN points to it in AI music and data-poisoning threads as the source for this technique.

title: Training an unbeatable AI in Trackmania
summary: Yosh trains a reinforcement learning agent to drive Trackmania until he can no longer beat it. The video explains how the training works and the design choices involved.
why_hn: Recommended as an approachable explanation of how reinforcement learning works in practice, and cited for the constraints needed to stop exploits.

title: CS231n Winter 2016: Lecture1: Introduction and Historical Context
summary: The first lecture of Stanford's CS231n Winter 2016 course on convolutional neural networks for visual recognition, introducing the course and the historical context of computer vision.
why_hn: HN lists it as a free, brilliant introduction to deep learning and computer vision, often within ML self-study plans.

title: A CGI 3D Short Film: "Dead Hand: FortressFortress/Крепость" - by Dima Fedotov | TheCGBros
summary: A 3-minute CGI animated sci-fi short by Dima Fedotov. An automated war system keeps a lone bomber attacking a long-dead city after humanity has been wiped out, until life finds a way to survive.
why_hn: Cited as a vivid illustration of autonomous weapons and machines that keep running after their creators are gone.

title: Joe Rogan Experience #1169 - Elon Musk
summary: A roughly 2.5-hour Joe Rogan conversation with Elon Musk covering AI, simulation theory, climate, his companies and his mindset.
why_hn: Recommended as a long, wide-ranging look into Musk's thinking, especially on AI and the future of humanity.

title: PREDATOR - Tracker that learns and improves
summary: A demo of PREDATOR (TLD), a real-time object tracker that learns the appearance of its target and improves while it tracks. The technology was later developed commercially.
why_hn: HN found it a nifty demo and cites it as a primitive but effective learning tracker that predates modern deep-learning trackers.

title: Darts in Higher Dimensions (with 3blue1brown) - Numberphile
summary: Numberphile talks with Grant Sanderson of 3Blue1Brown about a darts puzzle with a shrinking bullseye. Solving it takes the volumes of high-dimensional spheres, and the answer turns up Euler's number.
why_hn: Used as a friendly example of high-dimensional geometry showing up in a simple problem, and of ball volume shrinking inside a hypercube.

title: AI Live Painting in Krita - Interactive updates
summary: A short demo of interactive AI live painting in Krita using the Stable Diffusion plugin, where canvas changes update the generated image immediately. It uses an LCM sampler for speed and needs a high-end GPU for the interactive feel.
why_hn: HN points to it as a demonstration of local, controllable AI painting and a way to learn the workflow.

title: How China Tracks Everyone
summary: VICE News reporter Elle Reeve investigates China's rollout of facial recognition and mass surveillance technology and what it means for citizens. The report originally aired on VICE on HBO.
why_hn: Cited as a vivid demonstration of the scale of Chinese state surveillance, especially in TikTok and privacy debates.

title: Correlation CAN Imply Causation! | Statistics Misconceptions
summary: A four-minute minutephysics video arguing that causal models and causal networks let statistics infer causation from correlation. It touches on Reichenbach's principle, common causes, feedback and quantum causal discovery.
why_hn: HN people link it as a short, accessible summary of Judea Pearl-style causal inference when someone repeats that correlation cannot imply causation.

title: Sunspring | A Sci-Fi Short Film Starring Thomas Middleditch
summary: Sunspring is a sci-fi short film starring Thomas Middleditch. Its screenplay was written by an LSTM neural network trained on sci-fi scripts, and the team shot and edited it in 48 hours.
why_hn: HN cites it as an early, quirky example of machine-generated screenplays and what LSTMs could do.

title: What is PLUS times PLUS?
summary: 2swap explores lambda calculus using John Tromp's lambda diagrams, with animated beta-reductions, asking what PLUS times PLUS gives. It touches on Church encodings and the equivalence of Turing machines and lambda calculus.
why_hn: Mentioned in lambda calculus and combinator threads as a visual entry point to the topic.

title: MICRO DRONES KILLER ARMS ROBOTS - AUTONOMOUS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE - WARNING !!
summary: A dramatized fictional video of micro drones with facial recognition and swarm AI used as autonomous killer weapons. It is a Slaughterbots-style warning about lethal autonomous weapons.
why_hn: Linked in drone and military AI threads as a chilling dramatization, though some find it alarmist.

title: Did We Just Change Animation Forever?
summary: Corridor Crew explain how they made an anime short by filming themselves and running the footage through custom-trained Stable Diffusion models. The video walks through the technique and its open-source foundations.
why_hn: HN cites it as an example of temporally stable AI video stylization built from ordinary production gear.

title: God Mode (Person of Interest)(2 x 22)
summary: A short clip from Person of Interest season 2 where Root and John gain full access to The Machine and its resources. It shows the AI guiding people with targeting data.
why_hn: Referenced as a fictional illustration of AI-assisted tools and non-visual interfaces.

title: Neural Network Learns The Physics of Fluids and Smoke | Two Minute Papers #118
summary: Two Minute Papers covers a paper on speeding up fluid and smoke simulation with convolutional networks. It contrasts the approach with earlier regression forest methods.
why_hn: It is cited as an early example of neural networks learning physics, and recalled during later discussions of AI video generation.

title: Multi-Agent Hide and Seek
summary: OpenAI's short demo of agents playing hide-and-seek in a simulated environment. Through self-play, the agents develop six progressively more complex strategies and counter-strategies, including tool use.
why_hn: HN uses it as a vivid example of emergent behavior from multi-agent reinforcement learning, and as a way to make AI misalignment concerns feel concrete.

title: Epicycles, complex Fourier series and Homer Simpson's orbit
summary: Mathologer explains epicycles and complex Fourier series, inspired by an animation of Homer Simpson drawn with epicycles. It covers the shape of the Moon's orbit around the Sun and how to make your own epicycle drawings.
why_hn: HN points to it as a visual teaching resource for Fourier series, and as a reference when epicycles come up as analogies.

title: Swift for TensorFlow: The Next-Generation Machine Learning Framework (TF Dev Summit '19)
summary: Chris Lattner and Brennan Saeta present Swift for TensorFlow at the TensorFlow Dev Summit 2019, covering language-integrated automatic differentiation and tooling for machine learning in Swift.
why_hn: Cited as the source for Google's Swift for TensorFlow effort, later remembered as a once-hyped ML language.

title: Jeff Dean & Noam Shazeer — 25 years at Google: from PageRank to AGI
summary: Dwarkesh Patel interviews Google's Jeff Dean and Noam Shazeer about 25 years at the company, from PageRank and MapReduce to the Transformer, mixture of experts and Gemini. They also discuss where AI is heading.
why_hn: HN cites it for insight into Google researchers' views on AI progress and publishing, though one commenter finds the interview weak.

title: Tesla Autopilot Crashes into Motorcycle Riders - Why?
summary: FortNine looks at why Tesla Autopilot has rear-ended motorcyclists, speculating that the vision system misreads motorcycle taillights as a distant car. It argues that radar and other sensors would help.
why_hn: Cited in threads on motorcycle safety, Tesla's sensor choices and autonomous vehicles as a well-made explanation of the failure mode.
